title: Comprehensive Geriatric Assessment: Function, Cognition, Medications, Goals, and Supports
bottomLine: A comprehensive geriatric assessment is multidimensional. Evaluate medical problems together with function, mobility/falls, cognition/delirium risk, mood, medications, nutrition, continence, sensory loss, social supports, caregiver burden, goals and advance-care context; a disease-only visit can miss the factors that actually determine safety and independence.
recognize: Decline in ADLs/IADLs, falls, weight loss, confusion or medication errors may signal vulnerability before a single disease diagnosis is obvious.
Frailty and multimorbidity make treatment burden and functional outcomes as important as disease-specific targets.
differentiate: Chronologic age alone does not define frailty, cognition or independence.
A normal office vital sign panel does not mean the older adult is functionally safe at home.
assessment: Review ADLs/IADLs, gait/balance, falls, cognition, mood, medications, nutrition/weight, continence, vision/hearing, pain, sleep, social support, housing, caregiver strain, driving and goals of care.
workup: Use targeted cognitive, mood, gait/falls and nutritional tools when they clarify a clinical question; investigate new decline for reversible illness rather than attributing it to aging.
management: Prioritize the patient's goals, simplify treatment burden, address reversible risks and coordinate interprofessional/community supports.
medicationSafety: Perform medication reconciliation and deprescribing review, especially for sedatives, anticholinergics, hypotensive and hypoglycemia-producing drugs.
counselling: Ask what outcomes matter most—independence, symptom relief, longevity, cognition, avoiding hospital or caregiver burden—and align the plan accordingly.
followUp: Track function and supports as well as disease markers; close referrals and home/community service plans.
examTrap: Calling new loss of function 'normal aging' without assessing cognition, medications, acute illness and supports.
oneLinePearl: In geriatrics, function and goals are vital signs too.

title: Falls: Find the Modifiable Risks Instead of Blaming Age
bottomLine: Falls in older adults are usually multifactorial and are not an inevitable consequence of aging. After a fall or gait/balance concern, evaluate injury and acute causes, then address medications, orthostasis, strength/balance, vision, feet/footwear, cognition, continence, home hazards and bone health with an individualized prevention plan.
recognize: Prior falls, gait/balance difficulty, weakness, visual impairment, sedatives, hypotension and environmental hazards increase risk.
Falls can be the presentation of infection, arrhythmia, hypoglycemia, stroke, bleeding or medication toxicity.
differentiate: A mechanical trip should not automatically end the medical assessment in a high-risk older adult.
Syncope and seizure must be distinguished from a true accidental fall when loss of consciousness is possible.
assessment: Assess injury/head strike/anticoagulation, orthostatic vitals when safe, gait/balance, neurologic/cardiac clues, medications, vision/hearing, footwear, home hazards and alcohol.
workup: Use targeted ECG, glucose, CBC/electrolytes, imaging and specialty evaluation based on the fall mechanism and red flags rather than routine broad testing.
management: Use multifactorial intervention: strength/balance exercise, medication optimization, vision/footwear/home modification, assistive devices and treatment of contributing disease.
medicationSafety: Deprescribe or reduce fall-risk-increasing drugs when benefit no longer outweighs harm; avoid replacing one sedative with another.
counselling: Explain that falls are often preventable and focus on specific modifiable risks rather than telling the patient to 'be more careful'.
followUp: Reassess falls, gait and intervention uptake; refer PT/OT/home-safety resources when indicated.
examTrap: Assuming a fall is explained by age and missing medication-induced orthostasis or syncope.
oneLinePearl: A fall is a syndrome—find the risks you can change.
sourceBasis: Public Health Agency of Canada fall-prevention resources

title: Frailty: Reduced Reserve Changes Risk, Goals, and Treatment Intensity
bottomLine: Frailty is decreased physiologic reserve and vulnerability to stressors, not simply advanced age or multiple diagnoses. Recognize mobility/weight/function/cognition vulnerability, look for reversible contributors and use frailty to inform medication intensity, procedural risk, rehabilitation, discharge planning and goals—not to deny beneficial care automatically.
recognize: Unintentional weight loss, weakness, low activity, slow mobility and functional dependence can signal frailty.
Minor infections or medication changes can trigger disproportionate delirium/function loss in frail patients.
differentiate: Frailty is distinct from disability and comorbidity, although they overlap.
A fit 85-year-old and a frail 65-year-old may have very different risk despite age alone.
assessment: Assess function, gait, weight/nutrition, cognition, social supports, polypharmacy, recent hospitalizations and patient goals using an appropriate frailty approach/tool when useful.
workup: Investigate potentially reversible contributors such as anemia, infection, depression, medication burden, malnutrition and endocrine disease based on presentation.
management: Use exercise/rehabilitation, nutrition, medication simplification, falls prevention and anticipatory care; individualize disease targets and procedural decisions.
medicationSafety: Avoid rigid intensive BP/glucose or sedative regimens that increase falls/hypoglycemia without meaningful benefit; deprescribe thoughtfully.
counselling: Discuss what matters most and explain that frailty guides risk/priority decisions rather than defining worthiness for treatment.
followUp: Track function, weight, mobility and caregiver/support needs over time.
examTrap: Using chronological age as a substitute for frailty assessment or using frailty as an automatic reason to withhold all treatment.
oneLinePearl: Frailty measures reserve; age measures time.

title: Polypharmacy and Deprescribing: Every Drug Needs a Current Indication and Net Benefit
bottomLine: Polypharmacy is hazardous when medications are unnecessary, duplicative, interacting or inconsistent with goals and physiology. Reconcile the real regimen, identify each indication/benefit/harm, prioritize high-risk low-benefit drugs, taper when withdrawal/rebound is possible and monitor what happens after deprescribing.
recognize: Falls, delirium, constipation, urinary retention, hypotension, kidney injury and cognitive symptoms can be medication effects.
Prescribing cascades occur when a drug adverse effect is mistaken for a new disease and treated with another drug.
differentiate: Polypharmacy by number alone is not always inappropriate; multiple evidence-based therapies may be justified.
Deprescribing is supervised therapeutic care, not abrupt medication abandonment.
assessment: Obtain patient/pharmacy/caregiver medication list including OTC/herbal agents; review indication, effectiveness, time-to-benefit, interactions, organ function, adherence and goals.
workup: Use structured deprescribing/high-risk medication tools where helpful, but apply clinical judgment and patient priorities.
management: Stop unnecessary drugs, simplify schedules and taper agents with withdrawal/rebound risk; change one/few variables at a time when possible.
medicationSafety: Benzodiazepines, sedative hypnotics, anticholinergics, opioids, insulin/secretagogues and hypotensive drugs commonly require special review in frail older adults.
counselling: Frame deprescribing as optimizing treatment, not 'taking medications away'.
followUp: Monitor symptom recurrence, withdrawal and function after medication changes.
examTrap: Adding a drug to treat a medication side effect without first recognizing the prescribing cascade.
oneLinePearl: In polypharmacy, every medication has to re-earn its place.

title: Dementia in Older Adults: Establish Decline, Function, Cause, and Safety
bottomLine: Dementia is chronic cognitive decline that interferes with independence and cannot be diagnosed from one screening score. Establish baseline/trajectory and functional impact, obtain collateral history, exclude delirium/depression/medication and selected reversible contributors, classify the likely syndrome and address safety, caregiver needs, future planning and appropriate symptomatic/disease-specific treatment.
recognize: Memory, executive, language, visuospatial and behavioural changes can present differently across dementias.
Loss of medication, financial, driving or household independence may be more clinically meaningful than the test score alone.
differentiate: Delirium is acute/fluctuating with inattention; depression can mimic cognitive impairment; normal aging does not cause major functional loss.
Rapid progression, early gait/neurologic abnormalities or atypical age require broader evaluation.
assessment: Use patient and collateral history, cognition, ADLs/IADLs, mood, medications, neurologic exam, sensory status, driving, finances, wandering and caregiver strain.
workup: Use targeted CBC/chemistry/TSH/B12 and neuroimaging when indicated by clinical context; do not order exhaustive panels or serial imaging routinely.
management: Treat reversible contributors, use appropriate cognitive therapies when indicated, support function/routines, manage vascular risk and connect community/caregiver resources.
medicationSafety: Avoid anticholinergic/sedative burden and use antipsychotics only for narrowly justified severe distress/danger after non-drug assessment because harms are significant.
counselling: Discuss diagnosis at the patient's pace, capacity remains decision-specific, and advance planning is best before later loss of capacity.
followUp: Track cognition/function, safety, caregiver health and goals rather than repeating screening scores alone.
examTrap: Diagnosing dementia from a low screening score during an acute delirium or untreated depression.
oneLinePearl: Dementia is decline plus functional impact—not a screening score.

title: Delirium: Acute Brain Failure—Find the Cause and Protect Function
bottomLine: Delirium is an acute fluctuating disturbance of attention/awareness caused by illness, medication, withdrawal or environment until proven otherwise. Identify and treat the trigger, use orientation/mobility/sensory/sleep/hydration strategies and avoid restraints/sedatives when possible; antipsychotics do not treat the underlying delirium.
recognize: Hypoactive delirium is common and easily missed.
Infection, hypoxia, pain, urinary retention, constipation, dehydration, metabolic disturbance, medications and withdrawal are frequent triggers.
differentiate: Dementia is chronic; delirium is acute/fluctuating and can occur on top of dementia.
Asymptomatic bacteriuria alone should not be assumed to cause delirium.
assessment: Establish baseline cognition, attention/fluctuation, vitals, oxygen/glucose, pain, hydration, bladder/bowel, medications/substances, infection and neurologic findings.
workup: Use targeted labs/imaging based on suspected cause; avoid routine urine culture or head CT without clinical indications.
management: Correct causes, mobilize, orient, restore hearing/vision, support sleep/nutrition and minimize lines/restraints; use medication only for severe dangerous agitation when necessary.
medicationSafety: Benzodiazepines often worsen delirium except specific withdrawal indications; anticholinergics/sedatives are common precipitants.
counselling: Explain delirium as an acute medical syndrome whose cognitive recovery can lag behind treatment of the trigger.
followUp: Reassess cognition/function after recovery and review medication changes made during admission.
examTrap: Treating a positive urine culture as the cause of delirium without urinary/systemic infection evidence.
oneLinePearl: Delirium is acute brain failure—find the trigger before sedating the behaviour.

title: Late-Life Depression: Treat Mood, Function, Suicide Risk, and Medical Mimics
bottomLine: Depression in older adults may present with somatic complaints, cognitive symptoms, sleep/appetite change or functional decline. Diagnose clinically after assessing suicide risk, bipolar history, grief, medications, substance use, pain and medical contributors; use psychotherapy and appropriately selected pharmacotherapy while minimizing falls, hyponatremia, bleeding and anticholinergic burden.
recognize: Loss of interest, hopelessness and functional decline may be more prominent than reported sadness.
Depression and dementia can coexist; cognitive symptoms should be reassessed after mood treatment.
differentiate: Delirium is acute/fluctuating; depression is sustained but can mimic cognitive impairment.
Bereavement does not exclude major depression when syndrome/impairment criteria are met.
assessment: Assess mood/anhedonia, suicide risk, function, cognition, sleep, pain, alcohol/substances, medications, mania history, social isolation and recent losses.
workup: Use targeted CBC/TSH/B12/other testing when a medical contributor is plausible; screening tools support but do not establish diagnosis.
management: Use psychotherapy, behavioural activation/social connection and antidepressant therapy individualized to comorbidity, interactions and prior response; urgent psychiatry for psychosis/catatonia/high suicide risk.
medicationSafety: Start thoughtfully and monitor falls, sodium, bleeding, QT/interaction and discontinuation risk according to the selected agent.
counselling: Normalize treatment and avoid dismissing symptoms as aging or loneliness alone.
followUp: Review symptoms, function, sodium/falls/other safety as indicated and reassess cognition after improvement.
examTrap: Calling new apathy and cognitive complaints dementia without assessing depression and suicide risk.
oneLinePearl: Late-life depression can look cognitive—ask mood, function and safety before labelling dementia.

title: Anxiety in Older Adults: Rule Out Medical Mimics and Avoid Chronic Sedative Traps
bottomLine: New or worsening anxiety in an older adult deserves a medical, medication and substance differential before being labelled primary anxiety. When an anxiety disorder is established, psychotherapy and selected maintenance medications are generally safer long-term strategies than chronic benzodiazepine use, which increases falls, cognitive effects and dependence.
recognize: Anxiety may present as somatic/cardiopulmonary concerns, insomnia, avoidance or repeated reassurance seeking.
Pain, arrhythmia, hyperthyroidism, medication effects, withdrawal and cognitive disorders can mimic anxiety.
differentiate: Panic-like symptoms with chest pain, syncope or dyspnea require medical assessment before psychiatric attribution.
assessment: Assess onset, triggers, function, depression/suicide, cognition, sleep, substances, medication changes and cardiopulmonary/endocrine symptoms.
workup: Use targeted ECG/glucose/thyroid/other testing only when clinical features support a mimic.
management: Use CBT/psychotherapy and evidence-based maintenance pharmacotherapy as appropriate; address isolation, sleep, sensory loss and caregiver stress.
medicationSafety: Avoid chronic benzodiazepines when safer options exist; if tapering long-term therapy, reduce gradually to avoid withdrawal.
counselling: Validate symptoms while explaining why medical and medication causes need assessment.
followUp: Track function, falls, sedation and treatment response.
examTrap: Starting or continuing a benzodiazepine indefinitely for new late-life anxiety without evaluating causes or falls risk.
oneLinePearl: In older adults, anxiety deserves a differential and sedatives deserve suspicion.
